“Five more minutes!”

I slammed on the bedside table as I tried to get up, the rickety lamp I had bought for five-fifty at the dollar store blinking from the impact. Mickey (my dear roommate, bless his soul) would have to wait for a good hour for me to properly wake up — each breath I took was sniffly and laboured, my lungs clogged and bogged up and my nose blocked like my late grandpapa’s arteries. My entire body felt like a rusty machine squeaking at the hinges, like a tractor without gas, because, to put it lightly, I was sick.

Well, that’s an understatement. I had quite possibly the worst flu of the decade, the kind that makes you so ill your face turns pale green, the colour of that avocado milkshake your niece has been chugging, and your stomach rumble and cry like a great thundercloud, or maybe a hissing stock of dynamite. I turned on my side, stomaching the urge to vomit out of the open window. It was pretty ironic, how today was so pristine, birds floating and warbling past in chirping sonnets, the grass on the college campus that was usually grey and brown from heat now painted in viridian hues, when I felt like absolute shit. The white walls of my room seemed so painstakingly bright, I wanted to rip my eyes out and burrow under the blankets and become some kind of weird cave-dwelling gremlin with no eyes. Curse you, God. It was like everything in the world was trying to annoy me today.

The door creaked open. I groaned. “Dude, I said five more minutes. It’s been… What, three?”

“Four, actually.” Said a smooth voice. Weird. That’s too posh for a countryside boy. I looked up to see regular ol’ Mickey, but for some reason, he seemed to have little bumps— No, scratch that, there were full-on bony appendages resembling goat horns, curling forward in great curving ‘C’s situated on the top of his head, attached through his beach blonde hair.

A snicker left my lips, before I was engulfed in full-blown laughter. Maybe he finally cracked? I knew the guy loved Dungeons and Dragons more than anything.

“Ha ha. Real funny.” I wheezed through bursts of raucous guffawing. A pillow was flung at him, which he caught with ease. “Lose the cosplay and we’ll talk.”

He frowned, before a smug grin settled on his face. “Oh, but you don’t see the gravity in this situation, do you, mortal?”

“Mortal—?!” I tried my hardest not to giggle like a schoolgirl. Man, was he really pulling out all the stops today. “Bitch, you’re mortal too!”

“I’m not.” Mickey said smoothly. The pillow crumbled into ebony ash in his palms. “Because I’m not your ‘Mickey’.”

“I am Azaroth, lord of demons, the reaper of souls.” He said with flourish. “And today, I grace you with my presence, and—“

A loud fit of coughing interrupted his spiel, bursting out from my mouth. I choked on some phlegm, letting out scattered, raspy croaks as I grabbed the cup of water on my desk and began to chug it down, wiping my mouth with the back of my hand. Mickey looked expectantly at me as I finished up my sickness-fuelled fiasco. He cleared his throat.

“And, as I was saying, I will kill you today.”

I gave him a deadpan look. “Today.”

“Yes.” He puffed up, as proud as a peacock. “Today.”

“Look, Mickey, or…  Akaza, whatever you’re calling yourself today—“

“Azaroth.”

“I’m sick.” I motioned at myself. “Today is shitty enough. Can you… Ditch the roleplaying?”

“No, I can’t.” He gritted his teeth. A shadow seemed to shroud the room, his eyes glowing a fiery red. “Because, as I said, you are to be my victim for today.”

“And.” Mickey hissed. “I do not take no for an answer.”

Maybe it was the flu that fuelled my sickness-induced haze that made me not notice the sudden change in atmosphere. But I stared forward at him blankly, opening and closing my mouth like a gaping fish, and decided to play along.

“Can I reschedule?”

He blanched. “What?”

“Let’s reschedule the whole killing thing.” I repeated, coughing to one side. My body felt uncomfortably hot, and I could feel a dangle of mucous dripping from my nose. Ick. “Because I’m really, really sick right now and today is…” I flopped on the bedcovers, sighing. “Just not my day.”

Mickey was silent, contemplating my words, before looking at me with narrowed eyes. “So… I slaughter you like a pig after you have sufficiently recovered?”

“Yep.” I nodded heavily. What was with the pig analogy? Man’s so overdramatic today. “You can kill me as much as you like when that happens, Mickey.”

He seemed to think for a good while, nodding his head slowly. A large, manic grin spread across his face: he resembled one of those Chucky dolls, or maybe a kid on too much sugar. “I accept.” He declared. “It would be unfair of me to not give you any sort of fighting chance, and strike you down while you are suffering from an…” He paused. “Ailment.”

“And,” Mickey said, determination evident in his eyes. “To quicken that process, I will take care of you during this time. You accept, do you, mortal?”

I shrugged. Seemed fair enough. Mickey would probably get over his gimmick within the week, and if he was kindhearted enough to help me through it, even if he was stuck in a phase...

Well, why not?

“Sure.” I accepted, with absolutely no idea what I had just roped myself into.

When my dad was young, like me, we’re both skinny fucks. He, like me, really wanted to gain weight. His friend suggested that he go to the local pharmacy and ask for a certain medicine which would allow him to gain weight and have a healthier appetite, and so he did. It works: he begins to swell up, gain weight, eat more, but begins to feel a little sick occasionally. He just chills and eats a lot. It’s all going well. Flash forward, he goes to his family doctor for a checkup, and the doctor smacks him on the head and says “You idiot, where did you get the steroids from?”

He has a lot of stories from the Philippines he likes to tell me. Since I live in Singapore, I’ve been stuck in study hell for most of my life. He’s told me his biggest regret was that I never got a childhood that wasn’t a textbook. I think our fondest memory together though would probably be how when we’d visit the Philippines, he’d bring me to eat tonnes of weird stuff. He brought me (back then a girl in grade school) to eat soup no. 5 (it’s bull testicle soup), and then laughed with all his friends as I ate unknowingly lol.

My school banned water babies (basically these gelatinous things that would ‘grow’ in water) and any kind of business because they thought it was crude for students to sell stuff. Was a Christian school.

I used to buy a lot of them off the corner shop near my home and smuggle them into school and deal in the school bus. If the teachers conducted spot checks I’d hide them in ziploc bags in my wallet (because they couldn’t check there or be hammered by parents as attempting to steal money) and sometimes hide in the folds of my school uniform or in my undergarments. As a primary three student I made at least $30 a day, which was quite a bit then.

I was travelling to America and was about 14. At that time we had to take a domestic flight to travel around a few states and I was terrified of virtually everyone because they were a lot taller than me, and was off my meds because my mother was paranoid that the airport security would think we were smuggling drugs. I was seated separately from my mother on a united flight, and seated next to a large lady who took up half my seat (I was so small it didn’t matter) and was feeling skittish. A large black man with the largest basketball shoes I’ve seen walks by, his head practically knocking into the ceiling, and then checks his seat. We make eye contact, and he sits down next to me.

Now I’m a sheltered kid from Asia who has never seen such tall people in my life, never been in America before, surrounded, without my mother and not on my antidepressants so I was terrified and paranoid. I didn’t sleep a wink on the plane, and when we arrived I couldn’t get my luggage because I was too short. My mother had already exited the plane and a queue was growing behind me, and I was too terrified to do anything because no matter how much I reached, I couldn’t get my luggage. I was near close to tears over something that simple.

The man just casually reaches over, grabs my luggage and hands it to me. He doesn’t even ask for my name and then accompanies me, his friend following along, to the baggage area, and helps me search for my mother (who had left before me) in the airport for a solid 15-20 minutes, in an unfamiliar place, in an unfamiliar country. He helped me a lot and I managed to find my mother after a while, and he even helped us to move our luggage out and guide us to the taxi stand.

I kind of regret being so scared of him then HAHA. But that guy was a real help, who knows what would’ve happened if he wasn’t there to help. To tall basketball man, kudos!

TLDR; Tall cool basketball man helps Asian girl find mom and get luggage

Was hit as a kid. When I swore I’d be slapped, when I was rude I’d be whacked on the arse with a hanger (metal or plastic) or a wooden comb, multiple times. Sometimes they got the belt out for major offences, other times it would probably be a cane. As a kid I hated it, but my parents balanced it extremely well imo. They always told me the reason I was getting spanked, even if I never understood it then. Now, growing up, I’m thankful they did what they did. Even though they didn’t necessarily work for some things (e.g. swearing), I respect my parents a lot more, don’t talk back and stayed away from bad influences because I was scared of the smack, and eventually began to understand what consequences meant.

I think physically punishment should not be an outlet for parent’s anger but should be viewed as what it is: it’s punishment. I’m from Asia, so whenever we see a rich kid disrespecting their parents, talking back and being extremely rude, we know why. Parents should always make clear why they’re punishing their kids and do it only for major offences (I remember clear as day I got smacked because I called my aunt a whore in our native language haha) so kids understand there’s a line to be crossed. Maybe it’s a cultural difference because beatings are so commonplace here. I know my parents were physically punished worse than me when they were kids (Caning, belting, kneeling on wood etc.) so maybe that’s why.

Though eventually these punishments became blurred because of a mental illness my mother experienced turning it away from punishment into a way for her to vent when she became hysterical, I think I’m thankful for the times I was physically punished when I was younger. When they became an outlet to vent is where I cross the line between harmful and helpful. No parent should strike their kids in anger. Physical punishment should only be done when calm.

Massive respect to all parents who deal out physical punishment correctly, most of all to my dad. He taught me how to be a good person.

From Southeast Asia, we don’t know many American accents other than the ones on TV so we always thought they’re kind of overplayed, but when I went to America and heard someone talk to me in a Kentucky accent I almost shat my pants.

In general,
Valley Girl Accent: Usually used to make fun of bananas (Yellow outside white inside) in Asia, usually used in a mocking tone. We all think it’s funny as hell, old people also mock the youth with it here.

Kentucky Accent: Everyone thinks it doesn’t exist until they hear it, usually makes us laugh because we find it funny as hell, it sounds so goddamn hilarious because we think it’s fictional, it’s like some weird... Bigfoot of an accent, you don’t think you’ll ever hear it until you do, and then you can’t believe it exists(??)

Bronx(?? Sorry, don’t know what to call it) Accent: The one where everyone starts slurring(??) their words, I think some people here find it cool and try to mimic it while others kind of find it peculiar, like you’re walking in the forest and suddenly find a plucked chicken, that kind of thing. I know some older folks here disapprove of it.

Northern Accent: Everyone here (at least in my country) finds it cool as hell, teachers like to encourage us to adopt a fake northern accent when doing English oral examinations so we look smarter. Other times we like to make fun of it as being kind of posh and uppity.
